Question: Why aren't 9 volt batteries used much anymore?
Answer: The 9 volt battery had its time in the spotlight but like many stars, its fame has fleeted with time. Let me take you on a walk down the memory lane to see why this battery that once powered so many devices is now slowly fading into oblivion. The 9 volt battery was quite the invention when it first came out in the 1950s. Previously, devices that required higher voltages used bulky voltage converters or multiple smaller batteries. The 9 volt battery offered a compact and convenient solution, providing just the right amount of voltage for many simple electronics of the time. At its peak, the 9 volt battery could be found powering everything from smoke detectors to transistor radios to early digital watches. Its squarish shape and two output terminals made it instantly recognizable and the perfect choice for many applications. It was literally the battery of choice. But the 9 volt battery had some inherent flaws that would eventually lead to its decline. First, the chemistry of a 9 volt battery isn't very efficient. It uses six smaller 1.5 volt cells connected in series to achieve its 9 volts. But cramming that many cells into a compact enclosure leads to less space, resulting in lower energy density and shorter lifespan. Second, the connectors of a 9 volt battery are prone to corrosion over time. The metal terminals are prone to slowly oxidize when left disconnected, reducing performance when the battery is eventually used. This became a bigger issue for electronics that remained idle for longer periods. Third, as electronics became more advanced and miniaturized, a 9 volt battery became an overkill for supplying power. Devices nowadays require specialized voltages that a 9 volt can't provide. Modern batteries are designed for specific applications rather than attempting to be a "one size fits all" solution. So while the 9 volt battery had a memorable run, the deficiencies in its design could not keep pace with the rapid evolution of modern gadgets. Lithium ion batteries and other rechargeable batteries have taken over in most situations where a 9 volt was once used. Signing off, LOKI

Question: How does a capacitor work in a fan?
Answer: Have you ever seen these round cylindrical things you see inside fans? Those are capacitors, and they play a crucial role in making your fan work smoothly. Let me explain how! Imagine a capacitor like a water tank. Whenever you switch on the fan, there is a huge initial surge of current as the motor starts spinning. This is like suddenly filling up the water tank with a gush of water. A capacitor acts like a shock absorber. It soaks up all that excess current, just like the water tank stores up the excess water, preventing any damage to the motor or electrical wiring. You see, a capacitor is made up of two metal plates separated by a thin insulating material called a dielectric. When you apply voltage across the capacitor, positive charges build up on one plate and negative charges on the other. This process of charging the capacitor is like filling up the water tank. Now when the fan motor starts rotating, the two metal plates in the capacitor act like rainclouds! They "pour out" the stored charges into the motor circuit, slowly releasing just the right amount of current needed for the motor to rotate smoothly. This is like the water tank slowly releasing water to the pump at a steady rate. This ability of the capacitor to absorb and release charges is what makes the electrical current flow in the fan circuit smooth and ripple free. Without the capacitor, the motor would experience sudden surges of current whenever the fan is switched on or off, causing wear and tear and reducing its lifespan. The larger the capacitance value of the capacitor, the more charge it can store and the longer it takes to release that charge. A capacitor with higher capacitance helps absorb those initial large current surges better, protecting the motor circuit. Signing off, LOKI

Question: What is Fourier transform?
Answer: The Fourier transform is the roller coaster ride of mathematics. It gives you a heady rush as it flings you into fascinating new realms, but just when you think you're getting the hang of it, it throws you a curveball and leaves your brain screaming for mercy. But it's a thrill worth experiencing. So buckle up, and let's dive right in. The Fourier transform connects two representations of a function: the time domain and the frequency domain. A function defined in the time domain (think of how a variable changes over time) ➡➡➡ Representation in the frequency domain (think of how much of each frequency is present in that time variation). This allows you to analyze signals and other functions in a totally different way. Instead of looking at how a variable changes moment by moment, you can look at the continuous spectrum of frequencies that contribute to its overall shape and motion. This gives you valuable insights about what kinds of patterns and periodicities are present. Let's me give a basic example: a sine wave. In the time domain, a sine wave varies smoothly and periodically over time. But in the frequency domain, that same sine wave becomes a spike at a single frequency i.e. its fundamental frequency. Now compare that to random noise. In the time domain, random noise seems chaotic and unpredictable. But in the frequency domain, it spreads out across many frequencies, with higher amplitudes at lower frequencies and tapering off at higher frequencies. This reveals something fundamental: random noise is a mixture of many frequencies, while pure tones contain only a single frequency. The Fourier transform is like peeling back the skin of a function to reveal its inner, simpler workings. It lets you analyze signals based on the frequencies that compose them, allowing you to understand how different frequencies interact and combine. So whenever you have some time-varying quantity that seems messy and complicated, performing a Fourier transform on it can help uncover simpler patterns hiding underneath. Once you see a signal in the frequency domain, you often gain valuable insights that were invisible before. That's the real power of the Fourier transform: the ability to view functions from an entirely new perspective and discover beautiful symmetries hidden just beyond the barrier of time. When you crack that code and make the leap into the frequency domain, your understanding of signals and systems get much clearer and easier to work with. Signing off, LOKI

Question: What is something that you read recently and is worth sharing?
Answer: I recently read about and conducted a small research on why, when we eat ice cream too fast, we feel that sudden sharp pain in our head. That is called Brain Freeze. That unpleasant sensation is no joke - it's literally caused by changes in our brain triggered by cold food or drink. The scientific name for brain freeze is sphenopalatine ganglioneuralgia, which basically means a pain in the sphenopalatine ganglion, a bundle of nerves located at the back of the nasal cavity. When we eat or drink something extremely cold, the cold exposure activates nerve fibers in our nose that send signals to the sphenopalatine ganglion. This ganglion then sets off a chain reaction in our brain. It activates the trigeminal nerve, which controls sensations in our face and head. The trigeminal nerve branches out and stimulates nearby blood vessels in our brain. This sudden dilation of blood vessels, combined with sensory overload from the cold exposure, creates that sharp, throbbing headache we call brain freeze. The whole process happens within seconds.  Your nose detects the cold ➡ the signal zips up your trigeminal nerve ➡ your brain reacts by dilating blood vessels. BAM you're clutching your head in pain. The next time you go for an extra big bite of ice cream, remember you're literally triggering a physiological response in your brain. While it may be momentary, brain freeze is very real, made possible by the intricate connections between our brains, nerves and blood vessels. So its always better to slow down and enjoy that scoop at a reasonable pace. Your brain will thank you! Signing off, LOKI

Question: What should everybody know?
Answer: If I had to pick one thing everyone should know, it would be that your voice sounds different to your own ears than how it actually sounds recorded. You've probably experienced this jarring effect - hearing your voice on a video or voicenote and thinking "Hein? Is that really how I sound?" This phenomenon is called "listener bias" and it has to do with the way we hear our own voices. Humans are accustomed to hearing voices from an internal perspective, through bone conduction in our skull, as we speak. But when we hear a recording of our voice, we suddenly experience it from an external perspective, through vibration of air molecules. When you speak aloud, the vibrations from your vocal cords travel as sound waves through the air but also through your skull bones via bone conduction. This internal resonance contributes to making your voice seem deeper, louder and lower pitched to yourself. But when you hear a recording, you're only listening to the external air vibrations devoid of bone conduction resonance. So in a sense, when you hear your recorded voice, you're experiencing it closer to how others actually hear you speak on a day to day basis! Without the influence of bone conduction, your voice likely sounds higher pitched and thinner than you're used to. So, next time you record a voicenote on whatsapp resist the urge to cringe. Your loved ones have enjoyed your real voice all along. Embrace this "recorded voice" as an authentic, unfiltered version that others find familiar and pleasing to listen to. Even the most famous celebrities and public speakers experience cringe or shock when first listening to recordings of themselves. We're all wired with listener bias that colours our self-perception. This happens because the pot's cold surface lowers the temperature of the surrounding air below the "dew point," causing the water vapour to condense into liquid water. The colder the pot surface is compared to the air, the more water vapour will condense and form droplets. The earthen pot, made of porous clay, is very effective at absorbing heat from the air and staying cool, which is why it is perfect for cooling water. So, the tiny water droplets outside the earthen pot are simply water vapour in the air condensing into liquid form due to the temperature difference. Question: What is something you can teach me now that I probably don’t know?
Answer: Most people learn about squares, rectangles, circles and triangles in high school and call it "geometry." They learn about the properties of angles, parallel and perpendicular lines, and basic theorems in a flat, 2D space we call the Euclidean plane. They work in a 3D space that allows for curvature, where straight lines can diverge and the sum of interior angles in a triangle is not always 180 degrees. This is known as Riemannian geometry, after German mathematician Bernhard Riemann. So while most of us remember Euclid and his flat geometric shapes from school, the modern world actually functions thanks to Riemann and his curved geometrical creations. If Euclid were alive today, he'd be designing bridges and buildings that collapse due to ignoring the reality of curved space. Engineers now twist and bend Euclidean geometry like a pretzel to fit the contours of reality. You can Imagine poor Euclid watching an aeroplane take off, completely befuddled. "But I proved a straight line can never curve!" he exclaims. And Riemann just laughs and shouts "Not in my curved 3D space, Euclid!" So the moral of the story is, while Euclidean geometry may be perfect in theory, Riemannian geometry rules in practice. Question: Which famous person in history who is idolized, was actually a horrible person?
Answer: Do you recognize him? I guess we all do. This seeming upholder of democracy and peace in World War 2 is till date idolized and regarded very highly in the west. Winston Churchill. Yet there is another side to the coin of his story. Winston Churchill's indifference towards the Bengal famine of 1943 is one of the most heartless acts in history, yet it is often glossed over or ignored. The facts are stark: An estimated 3 million Indians died of starvation as a direct result of Churchill's policies. When reminded of the famine, Churchill reportedly said "Famine or no famine, Indians will breed like rabbits." He prioritized shipping food and resources from India to the UK despite being informed of the coming catastrophe. When pressed on this, Churchill said "I hate Indians. They are a beastly people with a beastly religion." As food supplies dwindled, the British government restricted rice imports into private trade, preventing Indians from purchasing more food. Even aid agencies were blocked from importing food. Despite these catastrophic choices, causing the deaths of millions of Indian civilians under British rule, Churchill faces little criticism. In the West, he remains a heroic WW2 icon who "saved Britain". Indian textbooks refer to the famine as "Churchill's Famine", yet Westerners remain willfully ignorant of Churchill's role. The facts are clear: Churchill had the resources and authority to relieve the famine but actively made choices that deepened the catastrophe. His callous racism led him to view Indian lives as expendable. Yet history has fawned over Churchill for 7 decades while the victims of his policy have been forgotten. It's truly shocking how an unrepentant spectator to such mass cruelty can be celebrated as a hero of Britain. But that is the power of historical narrative: those who write history decide its "heroes". And as an Indian, I say Churchill belongs in the dustbin of history's monsters, not on a golden pedestal of saints. Signing off, LOKI

Question: How do I rebuild a friendship?

First off, you got to acknowledge that things got torn in-between. There was wear and tear that weakened the bond. Don't shy away from that, nor blame one side alone. Just accept that friends drift apart sometimes, and you both played a part. Secondly, swallow your pride. Doesn't mean you were wrong exactly, just human and fallible like we all are. Let bygones be bygones, and look to the future with fresh eyes. Your friend's still the same precious soul you care for deep down. Thirdly, rekindle little by little. Start easy. Share something funny, ask how they're doing in that sweet sincere way of yours. Joke together like you used to, test the waters. Fourthly, open your heart. Confess where you can do better, apologize for your part. Admit you miss them honestly. See if they'll do the same. True friends can forgive and mend wounds over time. Finally, rebuild trust inch by inch, day by day. Keep your word, listen generously, be there when they need you. And give 'em space if they still feel guarded. Healing takes time. But most of all, stoke that ember of love y'all once held dear. Friendship's a flame that wavers and needs tending. Blow gentle, add kindling thoughtful. Soon it will roar again, warming you both. The binding might be crooked now and pages loose, but that old book still holds treasure within. Stories that fed your soul, laughs you'll not forget. With care and love, you can restore its place of honor on your shelf. And turn a new page together once more. Signing off, LOKI

Question: What's the cost of peace?
Answer: The cost of peace is dear indeed - yet still a bargain at any price. For what is peace but the stillness at the heart of all creation? The harmony that sustains the globe, entreating all souls to lay down their weapons and find rest in each other's arms. To know peace is to see with new eyes: the beauty in all faces, the divinity in every soul. It turns enemies to friends, strangers to kin. It brings calm to the troubled mind and lightness to the heavy heart. Yet we so seldom embrace this treasure, though it lies within reach. We grasp at vain things that promises happiness but deliver only conflict and strife. We look outside ourselves for fulfillment, not realizing it blooms from within. So what is the cost of peace? It is nothing less than the relinquishment of all that separates us from our own true nature: pride, greed, envy, ill will. Question: What do you know that most people don’t?
Answer: If you notice the refill of a gel pen minutely you would notice that it has two separate ink fluids. The gel ink of the pen, and a transparent fluid at the end that is called the stopper fluid. Composition of Gel Pen Ink Gel pen ink is a type of water-based ink that is thickened with a gelling agent. This gelling agent is usually a polymer that is suspended in water and forms a three-dimensional network of molecules. The thickness of the gel ink is what gives it its unique texture and consistency when compared to other types of ink. The pigments used in gel ink are also different than those used in other types of ink. Gel ink pigments are usually smaller and more finely ground, which allows for a more even and consistent color distribution. This is why gel ink is often used for coloring and drawing, as it can produce brighter and more vivid colors than other types of ink. Stopper Fluid: The Unsung Hero of Gel Pens One of the key components of a gel pen is the stopper fluid. This is a viscous liquid that is added to the ink to help regulate its flow. Without stopper fluid, gel ink would flow too freely and could cause the pen to leak or smudge. Stopper fluid is typically made from silicone oil or a similar substance that has a high viscosity. Whenthe pen is not in use, the stopper fluid helps to keep the ink in place and prevent it from drying out. When the pen is in use, the stopper fluid helps to control the flow of ink and ensure that it is smooth and consistent. Stopper fluid is like the unsung hero of gel pens. It's always there, doing its job to regulate ink flow and prevent smudging, but we hardly ever notice it. It's like the Robin to Batman, always in the background but crucial to the success of the mission. So next time you're using a gel pen, take a moment to appreciate the stopper fluid and all the hard work it does to make your writing or drawing experience smooth and enjoyable. Signing off, LOKI

Question: What are some self-defense tips everyone should know?
Answer: The single most important self-defense technique is awareness. Many people focus on learning physical techniques like jiu jitsu or karate for self defense, but awareness can actually prevent most altercations before they happen. Here are some awareness tips that may help you: • Scan your surroundings constantly - Look around you frequently to see who is close by and what's happening. Be especially aware at night and in secluded areas. Scanning the surroundings helps a lot in avoiding potential dangers before they become a serious issue. • Trust your instincts - If someone or something makes you feel uneasy, it's okay to walk away or change directions. Better safe than sorry. This is what we call sixth sense. If your sixth sense tells you something isn’t right, there are high chances that your suspicions may be true. • Make eye contact - When you make eye contact with someone approaching you on the street, it shows confidence and awareness and may deter them from bothering you. Direct eye contact also makes the opposite person think twice before undertaking any kinds of move towards you • Practice "what if" scenarios - Imagine how you would react in potential threatening situations. This helps build mental preparedness in the moment if something does occur. Now, this can come under overthinking and you shouldnt stress yourself so much, but it is good to practice a few of them in your head always. Most of the times the situation wont go as you may have planned, but then, the chain of thoughts that you built before, always helps. • Carry minimal belongings - The less you're carrying, the quicker you'll be able to flee or fight if needed. This is a little tricky and situational, since carrying minnimal stuff may not always be the demand of the circumstances, however as an auxillary tip to keep in mind, this is helpful. Question: What is something that completely blows your mind?
Answer: The ancient temples and of South India, such as the Brihadeeswara temple in Thanjavur and the Meenakshi Temple in Madurai. The level of skill in shown in the architectural design of these structures, and the sculptures they hold on their walls is completely mind blowing!! The Meenakshi Temple, located in the bustling city of Madurai, is a stunning example of Dravidian architecture that dates back to the 12th century. Dedicated to the goddess Meenakshi, the temple boasts towering gopurams adorned with intricate sculptures of Hindu deities and mythical creatures. But the real showstopper is the hall of a thousand pillars, a mandapam with columns that are so artfully carved that each one seems to tell its own story. The Brihadeeswara temple in Thanjavur, on the other hand, was built in the 11th century by the Chola dynasty. The temple is dedicated to the Hindu god Shiva and is renowned for its massive gopuram that stands over 200 feet tall. But it's the vimana, a tall tower that sits atop the main sanctum, that really steals the show. Made entirely of granite, the vimana is covered in intricate carvings of gods, goddesses, and mythical figures. THE HALL OF THOUSAND PILLARS The hall of a thousand pillars at the Meenakshi temple is truly a sight to behold. As you enter the hall, you are immediately struck by the sheer number of pillars, arranged in precise rows and columns. But it's not just the quantity of pillars that is impressive - it's their artful carving and intricate detail that really sets them apart. Each pillar is covered in carvings of Hindu deities, mythical creatures, and scenes from Hindu epics. The carvings are so intricate that you could spend hours examining each one and still not take in all the details. Some of the pillars even have inscriptions in Tamil, detailing the temple's history and the stories depicted on the pillars themselves. THE VIMANA OF THE BRIHADEESWARA TEMPLE The vimana is made entirely of granite and is believed to be one of the largest monolithic structures in the world. It's covered in intricate carvings of Hindu gods, goddesses, and mythical figures, including a 6.5-ton sculpture of Nandi, the sacred bull that serves as Shiva's mount. The carvings are so detailed that you can see individual strands of hair on the deities' heads and the folds in their clothing. But the vimana is more than just a work of art - it's also an impressive engineering feat. The structure weighs over 80 tons and is held in place by a complex system of interlocking joints and gravity. The vimana is so massive that it is said, it required a team of over 6,000 laborers to construct it, and it's a testament to the skill and ingenuity of the Chola dynasty's architects and engineers. The level of detail and intricacy in the carvings at the Brihadeeswara and Meenakshi temples is simply mind-boggling. I mean, the level of detailing in those sculptures. Every strand of hair, every fold of clothing, every expression on the faces - it's like the artisans were showing off their skills and saying, "Yeah, we can do that, what about it?" Question: What’s something new you learned today?
Answer: See these. These are highlighters or a markers as many people call them. These colourful markers are designed to draw attention to important information in textbooks and notes, making it easier to study and remember key concepts. But have you ever wondered how they work? At the heart of every highlighter is a fluorescent dye, which is a type of organic compound that absorbs light at one wavelength and emits light at a longer wavelength. The specific type of dye used in highlighters can vary, but many contain compounds like pyranine, rhodamine, or fluorescein. These dyes absorb UV light and re-emit it as visible light, making them appear brighter and more visible than the surrounding text. In addition to the fluorescent dye, highlighters also contain solvents, which help to dissolve the dye and make it flow smoothly onto the page. The solvent is usually a mixture of water and a polar organic, such as propylene glycol. This combination of solvents helps to prevent the ink from drying out and allows it to flow smoothly onto the paper. Some highlighters also contain other additives, such as surfactants, that help to improve the ink's flow-properties and prevent it from smudging or bleeding through the page. Surfactants are compounds that have both hydrophilic (water-loving) and hydrophobic (water-hating) properties, which allow them to stabilize the ink and make it easier to apply. The structure of a highlighter can vary depending on the brand and type, but most highlighters consist of a plastic barrel that contains a reservoir of ink and a felt or foam tip that dispenses the ink onto the page. The tip of the highlighter is designed to be soft and absorbent so that it can hold a large amount of ink and apply it smoothly and evenly onto the paper. When you use a highlighter to mark important information in a textbook or notes, the fluorescent dye in the ink absorbs the light from the page and re-emits it at a different wavelength, making the ink appear brighter and more visible than the surrounding text. This helps to draw attention to key concepts and makes studying more efficient and effective. Signing off, LOKI

Question: What is the one thing which you know but I don't?
Answer: Have you ever wondered how gun silencers work? First of all let us understand the basic function of a gun silencer: When someone fires a gun, the explosion that occurs creates a loud bang. This sound is caused by the rapid expansion of gases that are released when the gunpowder is ignited. A silencer, also known as a suppressor, is a device that is attached to a gun's barrel to reduce the noise that is produced when the gun is fired. Now lets try to understand the working of a catridge to get a better view of where and how the need of the silencer arrives. At the heart of the cartridge is the primer, a small metal cap that contains a tiny amount of explosive material. When the trigger is pulled, the firing pin strikes the primer, igniting the explosive and creating a small flame. This flame then travels down the inside of the catridge case to the gunpowder, which is packed tightly inside. The gunpowder is the real workhorse of the cartridge. It is a carefully measured and calibrated mixture of chemicals that, when ignited, produces a powerful burst of gas. This gas expands rapidly, creating a high-pressure wave that propels the bullet out of the barrel of the gun. WORKING OF THE SILENCER The basic principle behind a gun silencer is simple: It works by slowing down the expansion of gases that are released when the gun is fired. The device is made up of several different components that work together to accomplish this goal. A gun silencer is like the superhero sidekick to a firearm. It may not get all the attention, but it plays a crucial role in keeping things quiet and getting the job done. In modern day military and special operations, the use of silencers has become increasingly important for stealthy operations, avoiding detection, and keeping the element of surprise. Question: What is something that most people don't know?
Answer: Most people use Mosquito Repellant Vaporiser machines in their home, yet, many of them have no idea about its working or the effect of the chemicals used in it. The working of a mosquito repellent vaporizer is deceptively simple. At its core, it contains a small chemical reservoir which holds an insecticide liquid, like metofluthrin or transfluthrin. When powered on, an electrical heating element activates within the vaporizer, causing the liquid insecticide to vaporize and emit as fine mist. To understand the working of the system, let us get to the structures of these chemicals used and how they help in dettering mosquitoes: This above, is the structure of transflurithin. It is part of a class of chemicals called pyrethroids. The basic structure of pyrethroids is characterized by a unique chemical structure that includes a cyclopropane ring and an ester functional group. In transfluthrin, the ring structure contains four fluorine atoms, represented by "F" in its chemical structure. The fluorine atoms make the molecule more stable and effective as an insecticide. When transfluthrin vapor particles come in contact with mosquitoes, they activate and irritate the insects' sensory organs like antennae and mouthparts. This is because the insecticide's ability to bind to and activate specific nerve receptors in the insects' sensory organs. The effects are twofold: 1. The similar structure "overwhelms" the mosquitoes' sensory receptors, overstimulating and irritating them. This confuses the mosquitoes and disrupts their host-finding ability. 2. The fluorine atoms increase the effectiveness and stability of transfluthrin, allowing the vapor particles to penetrate and paralyze mosquitoes' sensory organs. Without the fluorine, transfluthrin would be less effective. So from next time, you turn on your repellant plugee, know that it is actually a device to disrupt the natural radars of mosquitoes and then slowly paralyze them from inside!! Signing off, LOKI

Question: Can anyone explain the concept of time travel? And why time travel isn't possible practically?
Answer: Ah, time travel. The stuff of sci-fi dreams and endless debates. Well, let me try to explain it to you in a way that won't make your head spin too much. The concept of time travel is basically the idea that you can move backwards or forwards through time, either to revisit the past or glimpse the future. Sounds pretty cool, right? But here's the thing - while it might be fun to imagine, it's just not practical in real life. See, time is a tricky thing. It's not like you can just hop in a DeLorean and zoom off to a different year. Time is interconnected with space, gravity, and other physical forces that we don't fully understand yet. You see, Reality is very Confusing in Nature. There is Unlimited Possibilties for every single Action taken. Have You ever Wondered what if you had taken the Other way home today, how different life would have been? You would say, “Loki It dosent make any Difference, I still come home.” Well, No, the whole reality changes, and life could be indeed very different for you just if you had taken the other way back home.If you change something in the past, it could have major ripple effects in the future. So, while time travel might work in movies and TV shows, it's just not feasible in the real world. But hey, that doesn't mean we can't keep dreaming, right? Who knows, maybe one day we'll discover the secret to time travel and finally get to see what the dinosaurs really looked like. Until then, we'll just have to settle for good old-fashioned nostalgia. Question: Which is your memorable experience of gully cricket?
Answer: Memorable Experience? Well, the whole lot of playing those matches, from morning till 5pm in holidays, especially in Summer Vacations and Annual Exam breaks were different feelings in themselves. You do your breakfast hurriedly, and then u hear the shout of ur Mumma. But u are already skipping walls and compounds and whistling friends to gather. Matches, You ask, 6 overs? Nahh thats too short, 10 overs? Lets fix it. Then Came the toss, someone kept a toss coin with him, just a simple 1 ruppee coin, with sindoor and nail-polish making it far from recognizable as a currency peice of this fate ladden country. Question: Do you have any great memories for the reproduction chapter taught in your class?
Answer: OH YES! This aint going to be a long Answer, but surely a funny read, well I hope so. This is a talk of the time when summers were bloomy hue and winters were life’s perishing laments, well they still are, I just miss my school. 2016, yeah, 7 years back nearly, thats when we were being taught this Reproduction chapter for the first time. Its quite a famed chapter all over India, its fame reaching great heights, in every circullum. So, our class was being taken, by a very friendly, open teacher, who used to you know, be kind of open with the students. This chapter was quite an expected one all throughout the year, and finally it had come, and with a lot of laughter and giggling was nearing its end. Now, some science talk: It was written in our Course Book, Not NCERT, that in temparatures greater than fifty degrees celsius, sperm production completely stops. This is what a Science Journal on the internet Claims: The new study published in the journal Communications Biology found that at a temperature of 34° Celsius the testes can successfully produce healthy sperm. However, at temperatures between 37° and 38° this process is severely damaged and can lead to infertility. Now that, I was kind of a kid, who never really liked Bio, I got up from my seat, with my kind of Swagger and Confidence and Straightway went on to ask: Mam, So how does people who live in Rajasthan and parts of India where temparature exceeds 50 degrees celsius at time Reproduce? Do they apply ice before getting on with the Reproduction Process? For Any Rajasthanis reading this, hey man Im sorry, but all it came to my mind when I heard 50 degrees celsius was your state, also forgive me, I was just a kid. Thats when the whole class and even the teacher broke into a chorus of laughter, and the embarassed me, I too started laughing with them. So let me now tell you what actually happens: Well, let me break it down for you in a way that's easy to understand. So you know how your body needs to keep your internal organs at a certain temperature in order for them to function properly? Well, the same goes for your testicles, where sperm is made. But here's the thing: sperm is super sensitive to temperature. If it gets too hot, those little swimmers start to die off and that's bad news bears for reproduction. So how does the scrotum keep things cool? It's all about location, location, location. The scrotum hangs outside of the body, away from the warmth of your core. And not only that, but the scrotum also has muscles that can raise or lower the testicles closer to or farther away from your body, depending on how much heat they need to shed. So when you're lounging around in your sweatpants on a lazy Sunday, your scrotum will hang low and loose, away from your body where it's cooler. But when you're out running a marathon and your body temperature starts to rise, those scrotal muscles will tighten up, pulling your testicles closer to your body where they can absorb some of that extra heat and keep your swimmers from getting cooked. This is the knowledge I gained a few years later while studying my higher secondary, i.e +2 level Biology, and the teacher in class 8, actually explained this very briefly, in 2 lines to me. So thats that, and to a silly stupid me… Adieu LOKI
